title: Meta's $50 Billion AI Data Center Is Reshaping a Rural Louisiana Parish
excerpt: Richland Parish teachers are pocketing $50,000 bonuses, local businesses report double-digit sales growth, and the investment that started at $10 billion just quintupled — but not everyone is celebrating.
body:
• Meta has expanded its Richland Parish, Louisiana data center investment from $10 billion to more than $50 billion, making the AI supercluster one of the largest infrastructure projects on the planet.
  • Teachers in the parish received bonuses exceeding $50,000 this year — up from $10,000 a year ago — funded by surging sales tax revenue tied to construction activity.
  • Louisiana businesses have won more than $1.6 billion in contracts from Meta since December 2024, and regional sales tax collections are projected to jump 22% in 2026.
  • Housing costs have spiked — rents have quadrupled in some cases — and economists warn the windfall could fade once the construction phase ends and a smaller permanent workforce takes over.

When Meta broke ground on a data center in rural Richland Parish, Louisiana, in December 2024, the price tag was roughly $10 billion. Eighteen months later, the company has quintupled that figure. Meta announced this month that its Hyperion supercluster campus will grow to 5 gigawatts of compute capacity, pushing the total investment past $50 billion and ranking it among the largest AI infrastructure buildouts in the world.

The expansion is landing in a parish of roughly 20,000 people tucked between the towns of Rayville and Delhi in the state's rural northeast. Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry and Meta confirmed the scale-up, which President Trump had signaled earlier this year following a meeting with CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

A Tax Revenue Tidal Wave

The economic impact has been immediate and dramatic. Richland Parish saw more sales tax growth in 2025 than in the previous 20 years combined, according to Grow NELA, a 10-parish economic development agency. Regional sales tax collections jumped 13% last year and are projected to rise another 22% in 2026. Tourism revenue in neighboring Ouachita Parish surged 68% in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier.

"The numbers are so staggering that it's difficult to put into words."

— Rob Cleveland, president of Grow NELA

The most visible beneficiaries have been the parish's teachers. Superintendent Sheldon Jones confirmed that Richland Parish educators received bonuses topping $50,000 this summer, fueled by sales tax collections tied to the data center construction — a five-fold increase from the $10,000 bonuses paid the year before. Jones said the money has been "life-altering" for teachers and their families, and for the first time in his 30-year career, every teacher the district interviewed was fully certified.

Local Businesses Riding the Wave

Meta says it has awarded more than $1.6 billion in contracts to Louisiana companies since construction began, a figure that stood at $875 million as recently as December. The influx of construction workers — currently 3,700, with a projected peak of 5,000 — has reshaped local commerce.

A coffee shop near the site has grown from 40 customers on a good day to over 130. A regional charter bus company expanded its fleet from 40 coaches to 102 to shuttle workers, with its drivers now earning over $80,000 a year in a region where the median household income sits at $42,000. Cory Bahr, a 2026 James Beard semifinalist for Best Chef in the South, said his three Monroe restaurants have seen "double digit growth" in sales.

"We've seen people from all over the world in our restaurants, multiple times a week. It's a golden opportunity for local businesses to capitalize on unprecedented growth."

— Cory Bahr, chef and James Beard semifinalist

Scholarships, Infrastructure, and the Community Package

Meta is also investing beyond the campus itself. The company has donated $5 million to Louisiana Delta Community College to create scholarships for data center jobs, and beginning with the Class of 2026, every Richland Parish high school graduate qualifies for a full scholarship toward any data center-related trade certificate. An additional $1 billion is earmarked for local infrastructure upgrades, including roads, water, and wastewater systems. Meta has also funded equipment for the Richland Parish Sheriff's Office and the Holly Ridge Fire Protection District.

On the energy front, Meta is covering the full cost of the data center's power, water, and infrastructure. Its agreement with Entergy Louisiana funds seven new natural gas plants, three grid-scale batteries, and nuclear uprates at existing facilities — a deal the utility projects will save its customers more than $2 billion over 20 years, on top of $650 million in savings from the original agreement. Meta has also pledged to return 100% of the facility's water consumption to surrounding watersheds.

Not Everyone Is Celebrating

The construction boom has brought real downsides. Richland Parish's tax assessor told local media that homes that rented for $600 to $700 a month before Meta arrived now command as much as $2,500. The New York Times noted that the sales tax bonuses could shrink once the construction workforce moves on and the campus transitions to its smaller permanent staff of roughly 1,000.

The tensions extend well beyond Louisiana. A Gallup poll earlier this year found roughly seven in 10 Americans oppose new data centers being built near their homes, with rising electric bills, strained water supplies, and lost open land topping their concerns. Dozens of jurisdictions across the country have enacted moratoriums on new data center construction.

The Broader AI Infrastructure Race

Richland Parish is not an isolated bet for Meta. The company broke ground last week on its first Canadian data center, a 1-gigawatt site in Alberta — the 33rd facility in its global fleet. The Hyperion project itself has grown through a joint venture with Blue Owl Capital that committed $27 billion in development costs by October 2025. Reports suggest Meta may ultimately spend over $200 billion on the Louisiana site, largely on AI chips, though the company has confirmed nothing beyond the $50 billion headline.

For the Indian diaspora working across American tech hubs, the Hyperion expansion underscores a broader shift: the AI infrastructure buildout is creating thousands of high-paying jobs and contractor opportunities far from Silicon Valley and Seattle, in regions where the cost of living remains a fraction of coastal cities. Once operational, Richland Parish's campus alone will support more than 1,000 permanent positions — double what Meta projected just seven months ago.
